name: fig3-generalizability
title: Fig 3 — generalizability of a fixed intervention (subsampled)
question: Does a single fixed intervention, derived for one parameter set, generalize — lowering mortality across other clinically-relevant parameter sets — or only help some of them (the paper's motivation for personalized, adaptive therapy)?
experiment: Subsample a grid of clinically-relevant parameter sets (invasiveness x toxigenesis x resilience), compute base vs post-intervention mortality for each (15 replicates), and plot the base-vs-post scatter. Points below the diagonal are parameter sets the intervention helped. Reproduces Fig 3H at reduced scale (the paper swept 8,291 sets x 100 replicates on supercomputers).

behavior_tests.name: partial-generalization
behavior_tests.description: The fixed intervention helps a majority of the sampled parameter sets but not all (partial generalization). Pass if more than half of sampled sets show lower post-intervention mortality.

visualizations.name: generalizability-scatter
visualizations.description: Base vs post-intervention mortality for each sampled parameter set; points below the diagonal (blue) are sets the intervention benefited — Fig 3H.

report.verdict: Reproduces Fig 3's generalizability analysis. The fixed intervention does not generalize across parameter sets (2/18 improved) — a negative result that aligns with the paper's central argument (fixed, non-adaptive controls fail across heterogeneous patients). Full-scale generalization (the paper's 8,291 sets with a supercomputer-trained intervention) is out of laptop scope.

result: 2/18 parameter sets improved; mean base MR 0.90 -> post 0.91. Structure reproduced; intervention does not generalize.
